- &gt; Prepare, in consultation with the City, and distribute an agenda prior to meetings and prepare and distribute meeting notes following meetings.

## Technical Issues and Approaches

The following section discusses work to be conducted and considered under each environmental topic. The discussion of each topic focuses on work and considerations specific to that topic..

## Technical Topics

## Aesthetics

The proposed project would introduce new residences on a hillside site that is currently undeveloped. The proposed new residential structures and landscaping, as well as proposed grading and vegetation removal, could be visible from sensitive viewing locations in the surrounding area such as the nearby Harry Barbier Memorial Park open space area and trails, and public roadways including I-580 and US-101. New sources of nighttime lighting at the site could also be visible from the surrounding area. Potential nighttime lighting effects and effects on views from key public locations will be addressed.

This section of the EIR will address potential effects of the proposed project related to aesthetics and visual conditions. Potential impacts will be evaluated within the context of existing conditions based on ESA's assessment of photographs, onsite reconnaissance, and proposed project development and conceptual development plan details provided by the applicant. In addition, up to six (6) digital renderings (i.e.. visual simulations) of bulk and massing will be prepared by PreVision Design as a subconsultant to ESA. The aesthetics analysis will evaluate potential impacts related to scenic resources, views, visual character, and light and glare. The analysis of impacts on visual character and views will incorporate a characterization of the existing visual conditions of the project site and surrounding area; accessible public views of other aesthetic resources in the area; a description of relevant regulations, policies, and guidelines governing views and visual considerations; and an evaluation of potential impacts, including the proposed project to introduce features that would detract from the visual character of the area, conflict with applicable policies or guidelines, or create substantial sources of light or glare.

## Air Quality

ESA will prepare a draft and final Air Quality &amp; Health Risk Assessment Technical Report (AQ/HRA Technical Report) that addresses potential air quality and health risk impacts of the proposed project, based on the criteria provided in the CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. The AQ/HRA Technical Report will provide and evaluate:

- &gt; Applicable environmental and regulatory setting information that places the project in the appropriate context.

- › Construction and operational criteria air pollutant emissions (e.g., reactive organic gases IROGI and oxides of nitrogen NOXI, particulate matter 10 microns or less in diameter (PM10], and particulate matter 2.5 microns or less in diameter [PM2.5)) using the most recent version of the California Emissions Estimator Model (CalEEMod), and compare those emissions against applicable thresholds maintained by the Bay Area Air District (Air District).
- &gt; A quantitative construction HRA using the most recent version of the American Meteorological Society/ Environmental Protection Agency regulatory air dispersion model (AERMOD) to estimate PM2.5 and DPM concentrations (and corresponding potential health risks) at off-site sensitive and worker receptor locations, following the protocols outlined by the Air District, California Air Resources Board (CARB), and the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (ОЕННА).
- &gt; Project consistency with the Air District's 2017 Clean Air Plan and the project's potential to result in other air quality emissions (e.g., odors) adversely affecting a substantial number of individuals.

Information from the AQ/HRA Technical Report will be incorporated into the ADEIR to describe and characterize the air quality impacts of the proposed project using the CEQA Appendix G criteria.

## Assumptions:

- &gt; The project applicant team will provide ESA with the required information to complete emissions modeling in a timely manner in alignment with the project timeline.
- &gt; Construction HRA will analyze DPM and PM2.5 from construction equipment, vehicles, and fugitive dust.
- → Operational HRA is not included in this scope and cost. An operational HRA (e.g. for emergency backup generators) will be included as an additional scope and cost item, if requested.
- &gt; Modeling of speciated total organic gases from gasoline-powered vehicles and PM2.5 from entrained road dust, for the operational phase, is not included. If such an analysis is requested, it will be included as an additional scope and cost item.
- → ESA will conduct one (1) round of modeling based on the project information provided to ESA. If there are any significant changes to the project description (such as new building locations or phasing information, major changes to the land use values or traffic study, or significant revisions to the construction schedule) that requires major modeling adjustments or remodeling of the project, additional budget will be required, and ESA will provide a revised scope of work for review at that time.

## Biological Resources

The proposed project includes residential development on the fringes of a densely wooded parcel that supports native and non-native vegetation communities. In our preliminary review of the site, key biological resource issues to be closely examined include: 1) the loss of regulated trees and associated consistency with the local ordinances and the General Plan; 2) the potential presence of special-status plants and wildlife species identified from the San Pedro Mountain area on the site; and, 3) careful documentation of special-status species that may not occur on-site, but are otherwise mapped or attributed to it (e.g.. a California giant salamander record from GGNRA lands, mapped on the site in Naturalist). We recognize that our assessment of biological resources will be subject to close public scrutiny. Accordingly, ESA biologists will thoroughly address these issues in our comprehensive evaluation of CEQA impact categories.

As a first step in our review, a qualified ESA biologist will evaluate natural resource data for the site and surrounding habitat in Marin County. We will review the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) California Natural Diversity Database, CDFW Terrestrial Connectivity and Linkages database, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) Information for Planning and Consultation database, and the California Native Plant Society (CNPS) Electronic Inventory.

as well as relevant professional publications, local survey reports, citizen science sites, aerial photos, and other available materials, such as the project arborist report.

Following data review, a wetland/vegetation ecologist and wildlife biologist will perform one site reconnaissance survey to study regulated biological resources that may be present within or adjacent to the site. The survey will be conducted by specialists who are qualified to evaluate the presence of rare plant and wildlife species and sensitive natural communities, including areas important for wildlife movement and as nursery sites. As requested in the REP. ESA staff will characterize and map vegetation communities and habitats on the project site. If present, the location of potential wetlands, waters, and/or riparian habitat will also be described within the development footprint and their locations mapped. An ESA Certified Arborist will also independently peer review the applicant's Arborist Report and provide feedback to the City. ESA will also peer review the applicant's proposed Guidelines for Development in Riparian and Watershed Areas.

On this basis, we will develop a targeted list of special-status plant and wildlife species with potential-to-occur on the site. This will be incorporated directly into the draft EIR biological resources setting section and will form the basis for our impact analysis. Our approach will summarize and evaluate consistency with federal, state, and local policies and regulations as they pertain to the management and protection of biological resources on the site. We will identify which impacts are significant and require mitigation to reduce impacts to below applicable significance thresholds. ESA's findings will appropriately consider the magnitude and certainty of potential impacts, be supported with widely available and accepted data sources, and will address CEQA mandatory significance categories related to biological resources. Mitigation guidance, when provided, will be based on state, federal, and local policies, with quantified performance standards.

## Cultural Resources and Tribal Cultural Resources

The ASC will prepare a draft and final Cultural Resources Survey Report and provide tribal consultation support for the proposed project. The City of San Rafael will conduct formal consultation with assistance from the ASC and ESA. The ASC proposes to undertake the following:

- → Conduct pre-field and historical research on the project area, conduct a records search at the Northwest Information Center (NWIC), the ASC library and archives, online resources, and examine available City of San Rafael data.
- → Contact the Native American Heritage Commission (NAHC) for a review of their Sacred Lands Files and a list of Tribal organizations that will be included in consultation by City of San Rafael. The ASC will assist with contacting tribes and assist the development of government-to-government consultation between the sovereign tribes and the City of San Rafael.
- → Conduct a field pedestrian survey of the 20.79-acre project area and any relevant staging areas.
- → Prepare a Cultural Resources Survey Report documenting the methods and results of the cultural resources survey.
- → Develop a GIS database with newly identified and updated site locations to assist with project planning.
- → ESA will prepare separate Cultural Resources and Tribal Cultural Resources EIR sections based on the ASC's Cultural Resources Survey Report and the outcome of any tribal consultation.

## Assumptions:

- → If any cultural resources are identified during the survey, ASC will prepare site records or site record updates on California Department of Parks and Recreation DPR523 Forms at a cost of $700 per resource.
- → No human remains are expected lo be identified.
- → A Tribal cultural monitor from Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria (FIGR) will be present for the field survey. The ASC will contract directly with FIGR to provide a representative.

## Geology, Soils, and Paleontological Resources

Key issues would be construction on undeveloped areas with some steep slopes. The EQ Zapp website indicates the project site does not have any active faults but is within a seismically active region due to regional faults. In compliance with the California Building Code (CBC) and local building regulations, a geotechnical investigation has been prepared that describes site-specific geotechnical conditions and provides recommendations to address geotechnical issues, as needed. ESA will peer review the applicant's geotechnical report and incorporate information into the EIR as appropriate. In addition, ESA will research potential geology, seismicity, soils, paleontological resources, and mineral resources related issues in accordance with CEQA requirements. The evaluation will address whether implementation of the project would result in significant environmental impacts. ESA will:

- → Review site-specific reports, maps, and GIS data published by the USGS, CGS, Marin County, the City of San Rafael, Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), and other sources to identify and summarize geologic, seismic, soil, and paleontological resources conditions at the project site and develop comprehensive understanding of site conditions to assess the potential issues relative to CEQA Appendix G criteria.
- › Identify the relevant regulations, building codes and standards, and local ordinances that would apply to construction and operation of projects, and determine the manner and extent to which compliance would address potential impacts. This will include discussing how the requirements of the CBC and local building codes would address seismic, unstable soils, and stormwater erosion issues.
- › Identify which, if any, impacts are significant, and present mitigation, where applicable and feasible, to reduce the impacts to below applicable significance thresholds.

## Greenhouse Gas Emissions/Energy

ESA will prepare a draft and final Greenhouse Gas (GHG) and Energy Technical Report (GHG/Energy Technical Report) that evaluates the project's potential GHG and energy impacts based on the criteria provided in the CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. The GHG/Energy Technical Report will provide and evaluate:

- &gt; Potential construction (short-term) and operational (long term) emissions of GHGs using the same methodologies and models employed in the AQ/HRA Technical Report.
- &gt; Project consistency with applicable plans, policies, and regulations adopted for the purposes of reducing GHG emissions, including the latest Scoping Plan prepared by the California Air Resources Board, Plan Bay Area 2050, and the City's Climate Change Action Plan (CCAP) 2030.
- → The wasteful, inefficient, or unnecessary consumption of energy resources during project construction or operation.
- → Potential to conflict with adopted plans for renewable energy and/or energy efficiency.

ESA will first conduct a consistency analysis of the project with the City's CCAP 2030. If the proposed project is inconsistent with the CCAP 2030, ESA will evaluate the proposed project for consistency with the Air District's four building energy use and transportation qualitative measures.

Regarding Energy. ESA will evaluate the proposed project pursuant to the CEQA Appendix G checklist for energy to determine whether development under the proposed project would have the potential to result in wasteful, inefficient, or unnecessary consumption of energy resources during construction and operation, and whether these conditions could conflict with or obstruct a state or local plan for renewable energy or energy efficiency. The GHG/Energy Technical Report will examine existing usage and assess the proposed project's effects on consumption of energy resources during construction and any changes in energy demand over the long term. If necessary, to reduce inefficient or wasteful energy consumption, ESA will identify mitigation measures that may include items suggested in Appendix F

of the CEQA Guidelines, including measures to reduce construction and transportation energy use, increase building energy efficiency, and reduce solid waste generation.

Information from the GHG/Energy Technical Report will be incorporated into the ADEIR to describe and characterize the GHG emissions and energy impacts of the proposed project in separate chapters using the CEQA Appendix G criteria.

## Assumptions:

- &gt; The Air District does not provide CEQA significance thresholds for construction GHG emissions; therefore, construction GHG impacts will be discussed qualitatively.
- &gt; Similar assumptions from the AQ/HRA Technical Report apply.

## Hazards and Hazardous Materials

ESA understands that the project site is undeveloped with no structures. Hazards and hazardous materials information will be acquired through literature and website searches. The primary hazards and hazardous materials issues would be construction activities. Although hazardous materials would be used during construction, the transportation, use. storage, and disposal of hazardous materials is heavily regulated and compliance with the law is anticipated to reduce risks of exposure. ESA will evaluate potential hazards and hazardous materials issues that have the potential to affect development activities in accordance with CEQA requirements. The evaluation will address whether implementation of the project would result in significant impacts to the public or the environment relative to hazardous materials. ESA will:

- &gt; Develop a site-specific setting of hazards and hazardous materials conditions using published reports and maps, along with other relevant reports. We will use the setting to identify the hazards and hazardous materials issues that could result from development activities.
- → Identify the relevant regulations, building codes and standards, and local ordinances that would apply to construction and operation of the project, and determine the manner and extent to which compliance would address potential impacts. This will include discussing how the requirements of the Hazardous Materials Business Plans, the NPDES Construction General Permit, and the Regional Stormwater Permit would address hazards and hazardous materials issues. The degree to which such requirements will reduce potential effects and any additional actions that might be required will receive careful consideration.
- → Identify which, if any. impacts are significant, and present mitigation, where applicable and feasible, to reduce the impacts to below applicable significance thresholds.

## Hydrology and Water Quality

The key hydrology and water quality issues of concern would be erosion and water quality impacts during construction and operations activities related to stormwater runoff. Compliance with the NPDES Construction General Permit during construction activities and the Regional Stormwater Permit during operations are expected to address stormwater runoff issues. ESA will peer review the applicant's Hydrology Report and Stormwater Control Plan and incorporate information into the EIR as appropriate. ESA will address the potential hydrology and water quality related impacts in accordance with CEQA requirements. The evaluation will address whether implementation of projects would result in significant impacts to the public or the environment. ESA will:

- &gt; Develop a site-specific setting of the hydrology and water quality issues through review of the Regional Stormwater Permit. other available reports, maps, and data published by state, county, FEMA, City, and other sources to identify and summarize hydrologic and water quality conditions within the City to develop a comprehensive understanding of potential issues of concern.

- › Identify and update the relevant regulations, building codes and standards, and local ordinance codes that would apply to construction and operation of the program, and determine the manner and extent to which compliance would address potential impacts. This will include discussing how the Construction General Permit, Regional Stormwater Permit, and low impact development (LID) requirements would address erosion and runoff issues.
- → Identify which, if any, impacts are significant, and present mitigation, where applicable and feasible, to reduce the impacts to below applicable significance thresholds.

## Land Use and Planning

The effects of the proposed project on community division and consistency with applicable plans (including, but not Limited to General Plan, zoning, and regional land use plans), will be addressed in the EIR. As a SB 330 project, the proposed project may not be consistent with every regulation within existing City plans and policies. As such, ESA will identify inconsistencies and determine if a potential physical environmental impact could occur because of any inconsistency. If there is the potential for an adverse physical environmental impact, appropriate mitigation will be identified to reduce or minimize the impact. In addition, under AB 1893, jurisdictions may impose certain objective local standards on Builder's Remedy projects insofar as those standards do not preclude the project from accessing the proposed density up to the maximums described in Government Code Section 65589.5.

## Noise and Vibration

ESA will prepare a draft and final Noise &amp; Vibration Technical Report. ESA will conduct a noise survey comprised of two long-term (24-hour) and up to four short-term (15 to 20 minute) measurements in the vicinity of the project site to help characterize the existing ambient noise environment focusing on existing sensitive receptors that could be impacted by noise from project construction and/or operations.

ESA will evaluate the proposed project's impacts to sensitive receptors in the vicinity during both project construction and operation. Using the Roadway Noise Construction Model, ESA will estimate the noise levels likely to be generated by construction equipment based on an equipment list provided by the project applicant, a typical mix of construction equipment for similar mixed-use residential development projects or using default equipment assumptions of the air quality model used in the analysis of air quality impacts. Predicted noise levels will be compared to standards contained in the City of San Rafael General Plan Noise Element and the Municipal Code; ESA will rely on thresholds from the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) if quantitative construction noise thresholds from the City are not available. Construction impacts will also be assessed in terms of the increase over existing ambient noise levels. ESA will provide a discussion of construction-related vibration impacts using vibration levels and thresholds published by the FTA that will address the potential for building damage to adjacent structures as well as for annoyance to adjacent receptors.

ESA will also analyze potential operational noise that may result from stationary sources (e.g. HVAC equipment) and determine the increase in roadside noise levels resulting from project vehicle traffic. We will use algorithms of the Federal Highway Administration's noise prediction model to calculate the change in noise levels due to project and cumulative traffic along up to eight street segments most affected by the project. The analysis will evaluate the project's operational noise impacts to offsite sensitive receptors using standards and requirements in the City's General Plan Noise Element and the Municipal Code. The proposed project is not anticipated to include operational vibration sources.

The Noise &amp; Vibration Technical Report will detail the tools, methods, inputs, and assumptions used in the noise and vibration analysis and present impacts to receptors. Mitigation measures will be proposed, as necessary, to address

any potentially significant impacts identifed, and the significance of impacts after the implementation of mitigation measures will be discussed. Noise meter reports, model outputs and calculation worksheets used in the analysis will be included as an appendix.

ESA will use the analysis presented in the Noise &amp; Vibration Technical Report to describe and characterize the noise and vibration impacts of the project using the CEQA Appendix G criteria. The section will include a summary of the environmental and regulatory settings, as well as the significance thresholds used, impact findings and mitigation measures identified. We will also assess the noise compatibility of the site for the proposed residential land use. The land use compatibility assessment will be an informational discussion only and is not a potential impact under CEQA. Pursuant to the decision of the California Supreme Court in CBIA v. BAAQMD, the analysis will focus only on the project's impacts on the environment (i.e., existing sensitive receptors) and the CEQA impact findings will not consider the environment's impact on the project.

## Population and Housing

This section of the EIR will describe the characteristics and trends of population, employment, and housing in the City of San Rafael and Marin County, and will describe the potential changes to population, employment, and housing that could occur with the proposed project. The section will include an evaluation of whether the proposed project would induce substantial unplanned population, either directly or indirectly, or displace substantial numbers of existing people or housing, necessitating the construction of replacement housing elsewhere.

## Public Services and Recreation

This section of the EIR will evaluate effects related to public services and recreation associated with development of the proposed project, including demand for fire protection, police protection, public schools, park and recreation facilities, and libraries. For each issue, the section will include a discussion of existing service levels and will assess demands associated with the proposed project. ESA will conduct outreach to service providers to establish existing service levels. The purpose of this analysis is to determine whether development of the proposed project would result in substantial adverse physical impacts associated with the provision of new or physically altered governmental facilities, need for new or physically altered governmental facilities, the construction of which could cause significant environmental impacts, in order to maintain acceptable service ratios, response times, or other performance objectives for any of the public services. Close attention is needed for the evaluation of potential impacts to parks, open space, and recreational facilities as the project site is located near the Harry Barbier Memorial Park open space area and trails, as well as the San Pedro Mountain Preserve and China Camp State Park.

## Transportation

The EIR analysis prepared by ESA will be based on transportation studies provided by the applicant and peer-reviewed by subconsultant Fehr &amp; Peers (Task 3.1). Fehr &amp; Peers proposes the following tasks:

## Task 1 - Project Initiation

Fehr &amp; Peers will meet with the project team to confirm updates to the TIS analysis per comments contained within Dominican Valley TIS Peer Review (Fehr &amp; Peers, August 12, 2024). These updates primarily pertain to:

- &gt; Trip generation to account for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) (Comment #2)
- &gt; LOS analysis, including updates per the revised trip generation (Comment #3) and new LOS analysis at the Grand/ Linden intersection (Comment #4)
- &gt; Adequacy of trailhead parking (Comment #5, Comment #6) and access (Comment #8)
- &gt; Emergency access evaluation (Comment #10)

- → VMT significance threshold (Comment #13)
- &gt; Other updates to the analysis as desired by the City

If necessary, Fehr &amp; Peers will update the scope and fee to reflect changes as part of the outcome to Task 1. Fehr &amp; Peers will provide a list of data needs, including Synchro files from W-Trans developed for the TIS.

## Task 2 - CEQA Impact Analysis and Documentation

Fehr &amp; Peers will utilize the TIS to conduct a CEQA impact analysis for the following impact areas:

- → VMT
- &gt; Plan consistency as it relates to the:
- &gt; Roadway system
- &gt; Bicycle system
- → Pedestrian system
- &gt; Transit system
- → Hazards due to a geometric design feature or incompatible use
- → Emergency access

To conduct the CEQA impact analysis, Fehr &amp; Peers will tier from the TIS with the adjustments or additional analyses as described below.

## Site Plan Review

Fehr &amp; Peers will perform a detailed review of the current project site plan. They will provide comments and recommendations, where appropriate, for improvements to multimodal site access and on-site circulation. Specifically, Fehr &amp; Peers will review the site plan in terms of:

- → Site access and interface with public roadway network
- &gt; Emergency vehicle access and circulation
- &gt; Vehicular circulation within the site
- → Public parking layout within the site
- &gt; Pedestrian access and circulation within and adjacent to the site
- → Bicycle access and circulation within and adjacent to the site

Fehr &amp; Peers will also qualitatively evaluate the off-site pedestrian, bicycle and transit network to determine if the proposed project would result in CEQA impacts to these facilities.

## Update Project Trip Generation

Fehr &amp; Peers will update the project trip generation from the TIS to account for the trips generated by the ADUs. Although the ADUs can be built by right, ADUs increase average household occupancy and result in increased trip generation. To account for the ADUs, Fehr &amp; Peers will utilize standard rates for multifamily housing published by the Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) in Trip Generation Manual, 11th Edition, 2021. This methodology is consistent with the methodology in the TIS.

## Update VMT Significance Thresholds

Fehr &amp; Peers will update the significance thresholds for VMT to be consistent with Table 7 of the San Rafael TA Guidelines, which identifies project generated VMT impact thresholds. For residential uses, an impact threshold of 11.4 homebased VMT per capita is identified based on 15 percent below the regional average of 13.4. This change to the threshold would not change the impact conclusion based on the reported VMT. Fehr &amp; Peers assumes no change is required to the project VMT per capita reported in the TIS.

## Open Space Trail Access

The proposed project in the TIS assumed a loss of existing on-street parking at the trailhead. To determine whether a secondary impact results from the loss of existing on-street parking at the trailhead, Fehr &amp; Peers will collect occupancy counts of on-street parking adjacent to the trailhead. Fehr &amp; Peers will collect this data during midmorning conditions (8-11am) on one weekday and one weekend day. Fehr &amp; Peers will use this data and the site plan review above to inform CEQA impact analyses relating to open space trail access and secondary impacts due to the loss of existing on-street parking at the trailhead.

## CEQA Documentation

Fehr &amp; Peers will prepare the Transportation section of the EIR that will document the data, analysis, calculations and results of the work above. If significant impacts are identified, mitigation measures will be developed to alleviate the impact. Fehr &amp; Peers will utilize the mitigation measures identified in the TIS and, if necessary, develop new mitigation measures to alleviate new impacts resulting from the tasks above.

## Task 3 - CEQA Alternatives Analysis

Fehr &amp; Peers will assist with the CEQA transportation impact analysis of two alternatives to the proposed project. Fehr &amp; Peers will assess potential impacts of these alternatives related to VMT, transportation plan consistency, transportation hazards, and emergency access. It is anticipated that this effort will involve estimating the trip generation for up to two (2) alternatives and conducting a planning-level emergency vehicle access evaluation for one (1) alternative with a similar level of effort to the emergency access evaluation described below under. Wildfire. Fehr &amp; Peers has assumed up to 72 hours of technical staff time to assist with the analysis of alternatives. If, after review and identification of the project alternatives, we estimate that the effort will exceed the estimated labor cost of this task, Fehr &amp; Peers and ESA will notify the City to determine any appropriate adjustments to the scope of work.

## Task 4 - Informational (Non-CEQA) Updates to Local Transportation Analysis and Memorandum

Fehr &amp; Peers will perform a supplemental non-CEQA local transportation analysis that tiers from the TIS and is consistent with City of San Rafael Transportation Analysis Guidelines (Fehr &amp; Peers, 2022). The supplemental non-CEQA local transportation will include:

- → New weekday peak period intersection turning movement counts and intersection operations Levels of Service (LOS) analysis at the Grand Avenue/Linden Lane intersection. Counts at the other study intersections were collected in February 2024, which is generally deemed acceptable and not within the window of potentially abnormal traffic patterns created by the COVID-19 pandemic. The LOS analysis will utilize methodologies from the Highway Capacity Manual, 6th Edition as applied in the Synchro software analysis package.
- → Updates to the LOS analysis of the study intersections in the TIS to account for the trip generation of the ADUs. Fehr &amp; Peers assumes that they will be provided with the Synchro software files used for analysis in the TIS using methodologies from the Highway Capacity Manual, 6th Edition.

- &gt; New cumulative traffic forecasts developed using output from the TAMDM travel demand model and new LOS analysis at the study intersections consistent with the analysis methodologies described above. This scope includes LOS calculation for one cumulative plus project condition.
- → Other updates to the analysis as desired by the City.

Existing plus project scenario operations will be compared against the relevant No Project scenario to assess if the proposed project results in new deficiencies using criteria identified in the City of San Rafael Transportation Analysis Guidelines; if new deficiencies are found to occur, improvement measures will be identified to remedy the deficiencies.

A stand-alone technical memorandum will be prepared to document the data, analysis, calculations, and results of the informational (non-CEQA) circulation system analysis. This includes one draft memo and one final memo responding to one round of consolidated comments (up to 8 hours of staff time to respond to comments).

## Optional Task 1 - Full Reanalysis of TIS

If desired and as an alternative to tiering from the analysis documented in the TIS, Fehr &amp; Peers can perform the work required for the EIR without reference to the TIS. This may include the following components listed in the RFP but not assumed in the base tasks above:

- → Collection of new peak hour intersection turning movement traffic counts. Note that counts in the TIS were collected in February 2024, which is generally deemed acceptable and not within the window of potentially abnormal traffic patterns created by the COVID-19 pandemic.
- &gt; Reanalysis of the project's travel demand
- → Reassessment of the CEQA Impact Analysis
- → New LOS analysis

Fehr &amp; Peers anticipates that a determination of the Optional Task will be included as part of Task 1 - Project Kickoff. A separate scope and budget would be provided depending on the final scope. An order of magnitude estimate is included as Optional Task 1.

## Utilities and Service Systems

The proposed project would result in an increase in development and population in the area, and consequently, would generate an increase in demand for utilities services, including water supply and distribution, wastewater collection and treatment, stormwater collection, and solid waste disposal. ESA assumes that the applicant would provide a Utility Capacity Analysis for water and sewer that identify on- and off-site infrastructure improvements that would be required for the proposed project. ESA will peer review the Utility Capacity Analysis and other relevant available documents to describe the existing environmental and regulatory setting and determine the potential effects of the proposed project on utilities and services systems. ESA will identify feasible mitigation measures for any significant impacts in the Draft EIR.

## Wildfire

The project site is located within an area of moderate fire risk according to Calfire's Fire Hazard Severity Zones. The State Attorney General has issued guidance on CEQA evacuation analysis stating that a quantitative evacuation travel time analysis of multiple scenarios is required for projects in high or very high fire risk zones. Since the proposed project is not located in an area of high or very high fire risk, a quantitative evacuation travel time analysis is not required. However, given the project's location within hilly topography and served by a roadway network of narrow and winding streets. Fehr &amp; Peers will conduct an emergency vehicle access evaluation for one (1) scenario. The evaluation will incorporate a planning-level assessment of volume to capacity to inform the relative capacity constraints and consider access routes to the project site, the adequacy of roadway geometries to accommodate emergency vehicles, and potential

strategies to improve emergency vehicle access such as temporary or permanent conversion of roadways to one-way travel. Mitigation measures may include widening of certain roadway segments, conversion of streets to one-way travel (either permanently or under temporary emergency conditions), and other spot improvements.

ESA will peer review the applicant's Fire Risk Assessment that focuses on defining the recommended extent of defensible space around the development and recommend removal of vegetation types within those zones.

ESA will incorporate Fehr &amp; Peers' Emergency Vehicle Access Evaluation and information from the Fire Risk Assessment into the Wildfire section of the EIR as appropriate.

## Other Topics

Since no impacts are anticipated for these topics, the EIR will briefly discuss Agriculture and Forestry Resources and Mineral Resources in the Effects Found Not to be Significant (Statutory Sections) section of the EIR.

## Budget Estimate

ESA also has extensive experience working on residential and commercial development projects. Notable completed projects include the 1251 S. Eliseo Dr. Project Homekey Housing in Larkspur, which was finalized on November 18. 2022, for Episcopal Community Services. This residential development under the Homekey initiative highlights ESA's ability to deliver impactful housing solutions. Additionally, ESA recently completed the 6765 Washington Street project in Yountville, which involves a peer review of a Historic Resource Evaluation for a commercial/retail development. This project demonstrates ESA's expertise in handling diverse development types, including those with historic and community significance. Another project, still underway, is our 1939 Market Street Project in San Francisco, mixeduse residential development that will include more than 150 residential units, residential interior amenity spaces and outdoor spaces. These examples underscore ESA's capability to manage projects of varying scales and complexities. making our team a reliable partner for the Dominican Residential Development Project EIR.

The following projects provide a sample of our applicable work. These projects reflect ESA's expertise in CEQA documentation and developing the supporting technical studies, as well as urban planning and infrastructure improvements in San Rafael, Marin County, and throughout the Bay Area. These projects also demonstrate ESA's experience working on highly controversial projects in San Rafael and Marin County.

## Donahue Highlands EIR

## San Rafael

The Donahue Highlands Master Plan was a proposed residential development in Marin County, aiming to subdivide a 49.8-acre site into 18 single-family residential lots, including three affordable housing units. The project requires an EIR to assess potential environmental effects, such as impacts on air quality; biological resources; recreational resources. particularly with regard to a fire access road used as a hiking trail; and hydrology. The Marin County Community Development Agency oversees the environmental review process, ensuring compliance with CEQA regulations. ESA prepared the EIR; however, due to the controversial nature of the project it was never circulated for public review or certified. The applicant abandoned the project and ESA is now preparing CEQA documentation (either an EIR or MND; to be determined) for development of the Fernwood Cemetery (also referred to as the Donahue Highlands Cemetery).

Duration: 2018-Present

Contact: Rachel Reid, Environmental Planning Manager, County of Marin

415-473-6863 | rreid@marincounty.org

<!-- image -->

## Sea Level Ruse Vulnerability Assessment

## San Rafael

To help guide part of the City's General Plan 2040 update, The City hired ESA to categorize the vulnerability of the City's shoreline and to provide a series of priority sites and improvement measures for their ten miles of San Francisco Bay shoreline, with varying levels of vulnerability to sea-level rise. Many of the areas with the highest vulnerability are disadvantaged communities, which rely on a series of pump stations and uneven shoreline berms for protection. This study built on the prior Marin BayWave assessment and used updated site surveys and recent updates to the State of California sea-level rise guidance to identify priority sites. ESA developed revised flood vulnerability maps. the assessment report, and interfacing with City staff.

Duration: 2019-2021

Contact: Theo Sanchez, former Planner, City of San Rafael, 415-725-1003

## Boyle Park Master Plan MiLl Valley

ESA is currently developing a new master plan for the City to preserve and enhance existing amenities at Boyle Park. The Master Plan will explore opportunities to preserve natural habitat and promote growth and sustainability of native plants. The park includes two baseball fields, children's play equipment, lawn area, group picnic/barbecue facilities, restrooms, five tennis courts, a tennis concessionaire office/pro shop, and two snack bars. The park is bisected by Warner Creek, a yearround creek that needs protection of resident salmon species. ## Stonestown Galleria Redevelopment EIR

## San Francisco

ESA managed the preparation of the Stonestown Development Project EIR, which will redevelop the area surrounding the Stonestown Galleria shopping center. The project includes up to approximately 2.930 residential units; 160,000 square feet of new retail; 200,000 square feet of office; approximately 100,000 square feet of hotel: 53,000 square feet of cultural, institutional, and educational uses; 4,000 parking spaces; 6 acres of open space; and infrastructure improvements. ## Rock Quary EIR

## San Rafael

Under contract to Marin County, ESA prepared a combined EIR for proposed amendments to the San Rafael Rock Quarry's Reclamation Plan and Surface Mining and Quarrying Permit, The quarry, located at Point San Pedro near the City of San Rafael, extracts greywacke sandstone for use as aggregate, road base, rip-rap, and other products. Due to ongoing impacts on the residential neighborhood that adjoins the quarry property, continued quarry operation of a rock crushing plant and asphalt batch plant had become matters of considerable controversy. Of particular concern to the site's neighbors were blasting, truck traffic, and a degraded view shed. Additionally, the EIR analyzed potential impacts of planned post-reclamation use of the site, which include cutting a channel between the 350-foot deep main quarry bowl and San Pablo Bay to create a lagoon and ship channel. A mixed commercial, residential, and marina development is planned for the site. The EIR was certified and the project unanimously approved in September 2010.

Duration: 2020-2021

Contact: Retired

## Oakland Waterfront Ballpark District EIR

## Oakland

ESA prepared an EIR to analyze potential impacts of development of the Oakland Athletics' formerly proposed new baseball stadium and mixed-use development at the Port of Oakland, including up to 3.000 proposed residential units. The project site is 55 acres and immediately adjacent and to the west of the Oakland ferry terminal. ESA's team of technical experts analyzed a full range of environmental issues for the EIR, as well as peer-reviewed technical studies prepared by others. ESA worked extensively with Port of Oakland staff throughout the process to ensure the Port's input, as a Responsible Agency for the project, was thoroughly incorporated. The work involved detailed transportation and air quality analyses, potential impacts on Port operations, and consideration of off-site transportation and connectivity improvements. Potential conflicts between recreational watercraft, commercial vessels, and ferries in the channel were also assessed. The EIR was certified in February 2022.

Duration: 2017-2022

Contact: Pete Vollmann, City of Oakland 510-238-6167, pvollmann@oaklandca.gov

## 901 Rengstorff Avenue

## Santa Clara County

The proposed project is an SB330/Builder's Remedy project that is requesting a Development Review Permit to construct a 15-story building with 455 apartment units and a Heritage Tree Removal Permit to remove 19 Heritage Trees, relocate five Heritage Trees, thereby replacing one 2-story duplex on a 1.258-acre site. This project is located on the east side of North Rengstorff Avenue, between Plymouth Street and Leghorn Street in Santa Clara County and demonstrates ESA's experience working on an SB330/Builder's Remedy project. The project site is split zoned in residential and industrial zoning districts. The development proposal would exceed the permitted unit count, density, and floor area ratio (FAR) allowed within the residential zoning district. The industrial-zoned portion of the site does not allow residential uses at any density and the proposed project would not be compliant with similar development standards required in the industrial zoning district. ESA is currently conducting analysis in an initial study to determine whether the appropriate level of CEQA documentation would be an ISMND or a focused EIR Duration: 2025-Present

## Downtown West Mixed Use Plan EIR

## Google &amp; City of San Jose

ESA recently prepared a complex, project-level EIR regarding Google's proposal for an 80-acre mixed-use campus in Downtown San José. The City of San José and Google share the goal of creating a new mixed-use neighborhood in the western portion of Downtown San José, near the Diridon train station. Including up to 7.3 million square feet of office space and 5.900 residential units, the project will also include 1,100 hotel and corporate accommodation rooms; 500,000 square feet of retail, restaurant, arts, cultural, and educational space; and 15 acres of new open space. The City of San José Department of Planning, Building, and Code Enforcement relied on ESA to meet their goal of preparing and certifying a comprehensive and legally defensible EIR on an aggressive schedule, including publication of a 1,350-page Draft EIR less than a year after publication of the NOP despite numerous revisions made to the project description while the analysis was underway. ESA's project management team met regularly with City staff and Google representatives, bringing ESA technical staff to the table for deep dives into complex technical issues when warranted. Technical analyses prepared by ESA staff addressed air quality, biological resources, cultural resources, GHG emissions, hazardous materials, hydrology, noise, and other resource areas. The EIR was certified, and the project approved in May 2021, and later was awarded the Environmental Impact Analysis Award of Merit for this project by the California Association of Environmental Professionals. ESA is now assisting with mitigation monitoring which involves tracking applicable mitigation measures and their implementation in association with individual permits/ actions being pursued to implement Phase 1 of the project. ESA successfully met the City's goal of preparing and certifying a comprehensive and legally defensible EIR on an aggressive schedule

Duration: 2021-2024

## Subconsultant projects

## General Plan Update &amp; Downtown Precise Plan

## San Rafael

Fehr &amp; Peers prepared an updated Mobility Element for the City of San Rafael's 2040 General Plan Update, a transportation section for a new Downtown Precise Plan, the EIR for the General Plan Update, updated Transportation Impact Study Guidelines, and an update to the City of San Rafael's transportation impact fee program. Work began in the spring of 2019 and the two plans were adopted in August of 2021.

The Transportation + Parking Chapter of the Downtown Precise Plan describes the multimodal approach and intent, a street prioritization network based on a layered network approach, and strategy recommendations for ride-hailing, self-driving vehicles, micromobility services, parking, curbside management, vehicle travel reduction measures, and wayfinding.

Key early deliverables included a VMT White Paper, VMT policy recommendations matrix, and VMT memorandum to City Council on the transition from Level of Service (LOS) to VMT as a new CEQA metric as required under SB 743. Fehr &amp; Peers applied the updated Marin County travel model to estimate 2040 VMT, road segment and intersection volumes for three General Plan alternatives and a preferred alternative that will be evaluated in the General Plan EIR. We identified 2040 transportation improvement projects for the General Plan based on the forecasts developed using the TAM travel model, an activity-based model developed by Fehr &amp; Peers pivots off the MTC regional travel model.

An update of the City's traffic mitigation fee program, the first since 2004, that incorporated updates to the project list, fee levels, and allocation by program category was approved by the City Council in October 2021. A major update to the Transportation Impact Study Guidelines, which addressed the transition from LOS to VMT and how both metrics will be addressed moving forward, was approved by the City Council in February 2022.

Duration: 2019-2022

Contact: Barry Miller, General Plan 2040 Contract Planning Lead, barry@barrymiller.net, 510-647-9270

## Sonoma County

Fehr &amp; Peers conducted the CEQA EIR analysis for the Sonoma County Airport Specific Plan in Sonoma, CA. The Sonoma County Airport Area Specific Plan (Specific Plan or AASP) updates and supersedes the Airport Area Industrial Plan, which was first adopted in 1984 to guide industrial development adjacent to the Sonoma County Airport. The Specific Plan Area (Plan Area) comprises over 800 acres that have since transitioned from primarily grazing lands and orchards into a predominantly industrial and commercial area that provides vital jobs, goods, and services for the region. This work includes recommendations for MTC PDA requirements, CEQA transportation assessment (VMT, other CEQA multimodal analysis, evacuation analysis) and Non-CEQA circulation system analysis. SCTA model validation and calibration was also conducted.

## Marin Municipal Water District Mount Tamalpais Prescribed Burn Project

## Marin County, 2024

The Marin Municipal Water District (MMWD) Prescribed Burn Project proposed conducting four prescribed burns totaling 303 acres within District holdings in the Mount Tamalpais Watershed. The ASC conducted pre-field and historical research on the Project Area at the Northwest Information Center (NWIC), the ASC library and archives, and examined available Marin Water data. The ASC contacted the Native American Heritage Commission (NAHC) for a review of their Sacred Lands Files and a list of tribes to include in tribal consultation. The ASC contacted tribes that were available to participate in consultation, coordinated field logistics with tribal members, and facilitated consultation between tribes and MMWD. ASC surveyed the Project Area and documented their finding in compliance with CEQA regulations. including preparing site records on California Department of Parks and Recreation DPR523 Forms.

Duration: 2024

Contact: Carl Sanders, Watershed Maintenance

Supervisor, sanders@MarinWater.org, 415-945-1189

## Marin County, 2023

Caltrans District 4 proposed replacing culverts along Highway 1 near Bolinas Lagoon and Tomales Bay. Heidi recommended consultation with the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, the culturally affiliated federally recognized Native American tribe in Marin County, and additional subsurface investigation when the final site location is chosen.

San Antonio Wetlands Mitigation and Conservation Bank Cultural Resources Study, Marin County, CA. Project Manager/Archaeologist. Heidi completed a Phase I cultural resources study for the San Antonio Road Wetland Mitigation and Species Conservation Bank Project in Marin County. The study included a literature and records search, contact with Native Americans, and a field survey. Archaeological survey identified nine cultural resources-three prehistoric sites, one prehistoric isolate, and five historic-period resources-within or immediately adjacent to the Area of Potential Effects (APE). Three of the sites are considered legally significant. The sites are part of the San Antonio Creek Archaeological District and have been recommended eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places. ESA has recommended avoidance of significant archaeological sites and consultation with the State Historic Preservation Officer, the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in determining whether the project would have an adverse effect on prehistoric properties and if so, what actions would be necessary to resolve or reduce those effects.

Marin Countywide Bicycle Parking Pilot Program Cultural Resources Studies, Marin County, CA. Project Manager/Archaeologist. Heidi prepared the Historic Properties Survey Report and Archaeological Survey Report for this local assistance project sponsored by Caltrans District 4. The project included the installation of eight bicycle racks in various locations throughout Marin County. The cultural resources study included background research and an intensive survey. The ASR concluded with a finding of no historic properties affected.

Lagunitas Creek Watershed and Devil's Gulch Cultural Resources Studies, Marin County, CA. Archaeologist. Heidi conducted a cultural resources study for Marin Municipal Water District's Devil's Gulch and Lagunitas Creek Restoration Projects. The Devil's Gulch study included a records search, field survey, site recordation, site evaluation, Native American contact, and successful consultation with the State Historic Preservation Officer on behalf of MMWD and the National Park Service. The Lagunitas Watershed project included similar tasks as well as additional coordination with the California Department of Parks and Recreation.

Mt. Tamalpais State Park East Peak Facilities Management Plan, Marin County, CA. Archaeologist. Heidi prepared the cultural resources assessment for this State Park management plan. The purpose of the study was to identify previously recorded cultural resources, including prehistoric and historic-period archaeological resources, buildings, structures, and places of importance to Native Americans located within the plan area and to outline procedures for future identification efforts prior to implementation of the plan. Heidi recommended additional work in regards to historic-era cultural resources related to the historic railroad and tavern on the summit. Heidi also recommended continued Native American involvement during the planning process.

San Anselmo Flood Protection Project, San Anselmo and Fairfax, Marin County, CA. Archaeologist. Heidi completed a surface and subsurface archaeological study for the San Anselmo Flood Protection Project. The project consists of the removal of two buildings over San Anselmo Creek and the creation of a flood diversion and storage (FDS) basin in Fairfax. Heidi completed a records search at the Northwest Information Center and a surface survey. Due to the heightened archaeological sensitivity of the FDS project area, Heidi completed a subsurface survey using a mechanical backhoe to exposes subsurface strata and further delineate the archaeological potential.

Brian Pittman is a Certified Wildlife Biologist with 28 years of practice leading projects with complex regulatory, mitigation, and construction/environmental compliance backgrounds. He is fluent in biological resources characterization and management throughout California and routinely coordinates with scientists, planners, and resource agency staff to identify and resolve issues affecting sensitive or regulated resources. Brian is trained in the permitting procedures and requirements under CEQA, NEPA, the federal and California Endangered Species Act(s), California Fish &amp; Game Code, and federal and California Clean Water Acts. He holds a 10(a) federal Recovery Permit for vernal pool branchiopods, California red-legged frog, California tiger salamander, and San Francisco garter snake; and he performs a wide range of focused biological surveys throughout the State.

## Relevant Experience

North Bay Water Reuse Authority, North Bay Water Reuse Program Phase 2 EIR/EIS, Marin, Sonoma, and Napa Counties, CA. Biological Resource Task Manager. Brian led ESA's team of biologists for this combined CEQA/NEPA document evaluating the impacts associated with the implementation of 14 individual water reuse projects seeking funding from the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation's Title XVI program. Brian also led the EIS/EIR biological resources analyses and the program-wide Biological Assessment to secure funding under the Title XVI grant program.

## Marin Municipal Water District. California Red-legged Frog Surveys, Marin County,

CA. Project Manager and Lead Biologist. The survey results informed which areas needed coordination with resource agencies to address potential impacts to red-legged frogs.

Stonestown Galleria Development, San Francisco, CA. Senior CEQA Biologist. ESA prepared the Stonestown Development Project EIR, which would redevelop the area surrounding the Stonestown Galleria shopping center with additional residential and retail uses. The Draft EIR was published in December 2022 on an expedited schedule and the FEIR was certified in June 2024 with no appeals filed. Brian worked closely with ESA's lead CEQA biologist to ensure the proper approach to the analysis, to provide senior-level QA/QC review, and to ensure that the analysis met the Planning Department standards.

City of Oakland, Oakland A's Waterfront Ballpark District, Oakland, CA. Senior Biologist. Biologist the EIR, as well as peer-reviewed technical studies prepared by others. BDI, Brisbane Baylands Draft EIR, Brisbane, CA. Senior CEQA Biologist. County of Sonoma, Kenwood Winery Project, Kenwood, CA. Lead Biologist. ESA prepared an Initial Study for the entity proposing the Kenwood Ranch Winery. Brian Schuster leads ESA's Northern California Air Quality, Climate, and Acoustics practice. Since 2008, Brian has been consulting in the fields of air quality and climate change for CEQA, NEPA, and Climate Action Planning. Brian has many years of project management and technical leadership experience, often for large, complex, and controversial projects. He has authored dozens of EIR chapters for Air Quality, Climate Change, and Energy for a wide variety of projects. He develops, plans, and implements Climate Action Plans (CAPs) for public and private agencies throughout California. Brian serves as CAP project manager or project director and conducts GHG emissions inventories, evaluates GHG emission reductions, authors planning documents, and engages stakeholders. He has extensive experience conducting pollutant dispersion modeling using AERMOD and CALINE, modeling emissions using CalEEMod, EMFAC, OFFROAD, WARM, and ClearPath (Brian is a former member of the SEEC technical advisory committee). Brian is also a member of the Association of Environmental Professionals Climate Change Committee.

## Relevant Experience

Marin County, Climate Action Plan (2015 Update), Marin County, CA. Project Manager. Brian led the update of the County's 2006 CAP, which was one of the first municipal CAPs adopted in California. Brian created new municipal and community GHG inventories and evaluated GHG reduction effectiveness and cost-effectiveness for existing and new measures to meet the County's goal of reducing GHG emissions to 1990 levels by 2020. He developed a custom, interactive reduction tool, prepared a new CAP document, evaluated broad climate change adaptation strategies, supported stakeholder outreach and community meetings, and provided CEQA process support.

Town of Ross, Upper Road Land Division Project, Town of Ross, CA. Air Quality and Greenhouse Gas Analyst. Brian prepared a health risk assessment for construction activities associated with the project and prepared a technical memorandum to summarize the results of the analysis. This work was conducted as part of the project's Subsequent Environmental Impact Report for CEQA compliance. The project proposes a three-lot subdivision of an 36-acre parcel off of Upper Road in the Town of Ross. Substantial grading and other site improvements are also proposed.

Stonestown Development Project, San Francisco, CA. Air Quality Technical Lead. Brian served as the technical lead for the air quality analysis for the project, which would include up to approximately 2,930 residential units; up to 160,000 square feet of new retail; up to 200,000 square feet of office; up to approximately 100,000 square feet of hotel; approximately 53,000 square feet of cultural, institutional, and educational uses; approximately 4,000 parking spaces; 6 acres of open space; and infrastructure improvements. The EIR also analyzed one variant to the project. Brian led the preparation of the air quality EIR chapter. The analyses includes criteria pollutant emissions modeling for project construction and operations and a comprehensive project-level HRA for construction and operational TAC exposure along with a cumulative HRA for all nearby existing TAC sources.

City of Oakland, Oakland Waterfront Ballpark District EIR, Oakland, CA. Air Quality and Greenhouse Technical Lead. Brian served as the technical director for the energy analysis.

Sonoma County Regional Climate Protection Authority, Climate Action 2020 and Beyond, Santa Rosa, CA. Project Manager. Brian led a team to develop the Climate Action 2020 and Beyond. This effort provides a consistent and comprehensive assessment of GHG emissions and reduction strategies for Sonoma County, educates the public, engages stakeholders, and creates tools and policies to implement GHG reduclion efforts for the future. He developed a regional GHG inventory and reduction plan for the 10 jurisdictions in Sonoma County, including nine cities and the County, as part of a joint regional effort. General Plan Update &amp; Downtown Precise Plan (San Rafael, CA)

Bob was the Project Manager leading preparation of an updated circulation element for the 2040 General Plan Update, a transportation section for a new Downtown Precise Plan, an EIR for the General Plan Update, and a subsequent update to the city's transportation impact fee program. Key early deliverables included a White Paper, recommendations matrix, and memorandum to City Council on the transition from Level of Service (LOS) to VMT as a new CEQA metric.

Canal Neighborhood Community Based Transportation Plan (San Rafael, CA)

Bob was the Principal-in-charge overseeing the update to the Canal Neighborhood CBP that was completed in June 2022 for the City of San Rafael. The Plan update included an extensive outreach based on teaming with Canal Alliance and a stakeholder group comprised of members from the Voces del Canal who were paid stipends for their participation and leadership of the Saturday community workshop. Key agency participants in the process included TAM, Marin Transit, and Golden Gate Transit.

TAM Countywide Transportation Plan (Marin County, CA)

Bob was the Project Manager for the inaugural Marin County CP that was adopted by the TAM Board in December 2024 in the planned 15-month schedule. The CTP established a long-term vision and goals as well as identified 15 detailed strategies with implementation elements. The Plan was developed through an extensive engagement process that included six meetings each with an Ad Hoc Board Committee, a TAC, and an Equity Working Group as well as focus groups and pop-up events throughout the county.

General Plan Update (Rohnert Park, CA)

Bob was the Principal-in-charge for an update of the 2000 Rohnert Park General Plan. The updated General Plan will reflect development potential on the outlying areas of the City as well as incorporate a vision for a new Downtown District in the heart of the City. Fehr &amp; Peers is providing traditional Level of Service (LOS) calculations to size existing and future roadways and to inform the City's update to its LOS standards as well as developing CEQA VMT calculation methods and standards of significance to respond to the requirements of SB 743.

Marin County Travel Model Update, TAM, (Marin County, CA)

Bob is overseeing development of an updated Travel Demand Model for Marin County. The model is being updated with new 2022, 2040, and 2050 horizon years. Fehr &amp; Peers also completed an Origin-Destination Study for TAM, the first step in the process, that provides updated information on travel patterns based on "Big Data" from mobile devices.

## Marin Civic Center Station Area Plan, SMART Corridor (San Rafael, CA)

Fehr &amp; Peers, along with BMS Design Group, led the City and the Joint Project Team in developing a station area plan for the Civic Center station in San Rafael. This station is an integral link between the Marin Civic Center and the rest of the North Bay. Critical issues addressed in this study included pedestrian linkages to the various uses within a half-mile of the station and traffic/transit operations along Civic Center Drive.

Novato and Marin City Community Based Transportation Plans (Marin County, CA) As Project Manager, Bob oversaw preparation of the Novato CBP and Marin City СВТР Update to identify barriers to safe travel and work to overcome them. Fehr &amp; Peers simultaneously led both Community-Based Transportation Plan efforts, completing a collaborative planning process that invoived the residents of two lowincome Bay Area communities, the community and faith-based organizations that serve them, transit operators, county and city agency staff, and MTC. Fehr &amp; Peers worked closely with residents and stakeholders to identify transportation gaps, and then developed and prioritized solutions based on effectiveness and feasibility.

## Broadway District Specific Plan EIR (American Canyon, CA)

Bob Grandy was the Project Manager for the transportation assessment for the Broadway District Specific Plan EIR that evaluated the planned transformation of the City of American Canyon's core commercial along SR 29 districted into a more pedestrian oriented town center. The CEQA transportation assessment included an evaluation of 1,200 new dwelling units and 840,000 square feet of new commercial land uses as well as multi-modal streetscape design improvements.

## General Plan Update (St. Helena, CA)

Bob was the Principal-in-charge of a recently completed effort to prepare the EIR Transportation section for the Saint Helena General Plan Update. Fehr &amp; Peers was retained to quickly deliver a technically robust CEQA analysis of the updated General Plan, which had languished for a decade. Fehr &amp; Peers completed a LOS-based evaluation of the capacity of the circulation system and a SB 743-compliant analysis of VMT generated by the 1993 General Plan and the updated General Plan.

North Coast Land Holdings (aka former Baptist Seminary) EIR (Marin County, CA) Bob is the Project Manager leading the preparation of the CEQA transportation assessment for the North Coast Land Holdings project in the Strawberry area of Marin County. The CEQA evaluation will include a VMT assessment of a primary land use plan and two alternative land use options with varying levels of residential units. The assessment will be conducted using the TAMDM travel demand model.

## About

Neil has over a decade of experience in transportation and land use planning across Northern California, advising clients on sustainable growth and navigating the complex transportation landscape. As a strategic project manager, he excels in leading multidisciplinary teams on diverse project types, including transportation plans, infrastructure planning, and impact assessments. San Rafael General Plan &amp; EIR (San Rafael, CA)

San Rafael Public Works On-Call (San Rafael, CA)

He advised on urban design, sustainability, TDM, parking, infrastructure sizing, and regulatory strategies while managing stakeholder relationships, consultant procurement, and project commitments. ## SAN RAFAEL CITY COUNCIL AGENDA REPORT

Department: Fire

Prepared by: Paul Bernard, Battalion Chief

Thomas Wong, Sr. Mgmt. Analyst

City Manager Approval:

TOPIC:

REPLACEMENT OF FIRE HOSES AND NOZZLES

SUBJECT:    RESOLUTION  AUTHORIZING  THE  CITY  MANAGER  TO  EXECUTE  PURCHASE ORDERS  FOR  FIREFIGHTING  HOSES  FROM  L.N.  CURTIS  &amp;  SONS,  INC.,  IN  AN AMOUNT  NOT  TO  EXCEED  $82,506,  AND  FOR  HOSES  AND  NOZZLES  FROM ALLSTAR FIRE EQUIPMENT INC., IN AN AMOUNT NOT TO EXCEED $152,718

## RECOMMENDATION:

Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute purchase  orders  for  firefighting  hoses  from  L.N.  Curtis  &amp;  Sons,  Inc.,  in  an  amount  not  to  exceed $82,506,  and  for  hoses  and  nozzles  from  Allstar  Fire  Equipment  Inc.,  in  an  amount  not  to  exceed $152,718.

## BACKGROUND:

The delivery of water to a fire scene is made possible through two critical tools: fire hoses and nozzles. Fire hoses  transport  water  from  the  pump  on  the  fire  apparatus  to  the  nozzle,  which  the  firefighter controls  to  apply  water  directly  to  the  fire.  Both  components  are  essential  to  effective  firefighting operations, and the performance of each directly impacts the safety and success of fire suppression efforts.

San Rafael fire engines come equipped with a standard complement of nozzles. These nozzles are typically replaced when a fire apparatus is replaced or when nozzles become worn from regular use. Much of the current nozzle inventory in the San Rafael Fire Department is approaching the end of its service life due to wear and tear, as well as the unavailability of replacement parts for older models. To maintain optimal firefighting performance, the Fire Department is seeking to replace its most frequently used nozzles.

Fire hoses are another vital piece of equipment carried by San Rafael fire engines, with each engine equipped with over three-quarters of a mile of various hose sizes. Only three of the department's nine fire  engines  currently  meet  the  National  Fire  Protection  Association's  (NFPA)  recommended  10-year lifespan for hoses, meaning a significant portion of our hose inventory is overdue for replacement.

\_

Council Meeting:

Disposition:

SAN RAFAEL

<!-- image -->

## SAN RAFAEL CITY COUNCIL AGENDA REPORT / Page: 2

For optimal performance, nozzles must be correctly matched with compatible fire hoses to deliver water at the desired flow rate, pressure, and spray pattern. Currently, San Rafael's hose inventory does not meet  the  specifications  required  by  the  new  nozzles,  which  hinders  the  Fire  Department's  ability  to maximize  the  efficiency  and  effectiveness  of  our  firefighting  operations.  Replacing  outdated hoses alongside the nozzles will ensure the system functions cohesively, delivering the required water flow and pressure to safely and efficiently suppress fires.

## ANALYSIS:

A committee of Fire Department members conducted a thorough evaluation of fire hoses from three reputable  suppliers:  Key Hose,  Matex,  and  American Hose.  After  extensive  testing  and  review,  the committee unanimously selected Key Hose as the preferred supplier due to its superior performance, particularly  at  lower  operating  pressures.  This  is  a  critical  factor  in  ensuring  consistent  and  reliable water delivery during fire suppression operations.

Key Hose was chosen based on several key factors:

- Maneuverability  and  Handling: The hoses  demonstrated  excellent  ease  of  handling  for firefighters, enabling them to perform efficiently in high-stress, dynamic environments.
- Resistance to Kinks: Key Hose exhibited a significant reduction in kinking compared to other options, which improves water flow consistency and enhances operational effectiveness.
- Adaptability: The hose easily integrates with our current fire apparatus configurations, minimizing the need for costly or time-consuming modifications to our existing equipment.

New nozzles have been carefully selected for their higher water stream performance, simpler design, easier  maintenance,  and  overall  lower  cost,  making  them  both  operationally  effective  and  fiscally responsible.

Purchasing hoses and nozzles concurrently will ensure full compatibility between the hose and nozzle systems, improving water flow and delivery performance. The Fire Department will also benefit from increased  operational  reliability  and  enhanced  firefighting  capabilities,  leading  to  more  effective responses to emergencies.

The Fire Department issued a formal request for bids in accordance with City's Purchasing guidelines on  August  18,  2025.  Four  bids  were  received  by  the  deadline  of  September  9,  2025.  Bids  were submitted by Key Hose, Elkhart Nozzles, Allstar Fire Equipment, L.N. Curtis &amp; Sons, Inc. The low bid for Snap-tite hose was received from L.N. Curtis &amp; Sons, Inc.

Both selected vendors were found to have been responsive and have provided quotes matching their bids, as attached.

## FISCAL IMPACT:

The total cost of purchasing hoses and nozzles is $235,224. Funding is provided through appropriations included in the FY 2025-26 approved budget, within the Fire Department Equipment Replacement Fund (Fund 625). While funding is available for this purchase, future Fire Department equipment replacement needs  exceed  the  available  balance  (Fund  625).  This  shortfall  is  estimated  to  increase  by  about $170,000 annually, which will require the City to identify and secure additional revenues.

## OPTIONS:

The City Council has the following options to consider:

1. Adopt  the  resolution  authorizing  the  city  manager  to  execute  purchase  orders  for  firefighting

## SAN RAFAEL CITY COUNCIL AGENDA REPORT / Page: 3

hoses from L.N. Curtis &amp; Sons, Inc., in an amount not to exceed $82,506, and for hoses and nozzles from Allstar Fire Equipment Inc., in an amount not to exceed $152,718.

2. Do not adopt the resolution approving the purchases.

## RECOMMENDED ACTION:

Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute purchase  orders  for  firefighting  hoses  from  L.N.  Curtis  &amp;  Sons,  Inc.,  in  an  amount  not  to  exceed $82,506,  and  for  hoses  and  nozzles  from  Allstar  Fire  Equipment  Inc.,  in  an  amount  not  to  exceed $152,718.

TOPIC:

WIRELESS ACCESS POINT UPGRADE

SUBJECT:      RESOLUTION  AUTHORIZING  THE  CITY  MANAGER  TO  EXECUTE  A  PURCHASE ORDER FOR THE REPLACEMENT OF WIRELESS ACCESS POINTS, IN AN AMOUNT NOT TO EXCEED $128,299

## RECOMMENDATION:

Staff recommends that the City Council adopt a resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute the purchase of replacement wireless access points in an amount not to exceed $128,299.

## BACKGROUND:

Wireless  access  points  (WAPs)  are  critical  for  providing  reliable  and  high-speed  internet  access  for mobile devices throughout the City's facilities. With the increasing reliance on digital services and online platforms for both staff and public use, maintaining an efficient and up-to-date Wi-Fi network is essential to  support  a  mobile-friendly  workforce.  The  City's  current  Wi-Fi  network  was  last  comprehensively updated before 2020 and is no longer supported by Cisco Systems. This purchase allows us to ensure robust and uniform connectivity across all facilities, supporting the digital infrastructure necessary for the City's operations and public services.

## ANALYSIS:

This upgrade is necessary because the previous wireless system has reached its end of life and is no longer  supported  by  Cisco  Systems.  This  lack  of  support  presented  challenges  to  maintaining  the reliability and security of the City's Wi-Fi network. By upgrading to the Meraki Catalyst access points, the City will benefit from significant improvements to the network, including advanced monitoring and cloud capabilities, allowing for real-time management and troubleshooting.

The  cloud-based  system  offers  enhanced  visibility  into  network  performance,  enabling  the  prompt identification and resolution of any issues. Additionally, the Meraki Catalyst access points will deliver more robust and reliable connectivity, supporting the increasing demand for high-speed internet access across all City facilities.

This  quote  represents  the  balance  of  remaining wireless access points at other facilities that need to be upgraded to ensure consistency across our network.

## FISCAL IMPACT:

The total amount of the proposed purchase is $128,299. Funding to support this purchase is provided within the approved fiscal year (FY) 2025-26 budget through appropriations within the Technology Fund (Fund 612). This purchase does not require a new agreement because the managed service agreement with Xantrion includes the maintenance of existing networks and technology.

## OPTIONS:

The City Council has the following options to consider:

1. Adopt a resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute the purchase of replacement wireless access points in an amount not to exceed $128,299.
2. Direct staff to return with more information.
3. Take no action.

TOPIC:

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SERVICES AGREEMENT RENEWAL

SUBJECT:      RESOLUTION  AUTHORIZING  THE  CITY  MANAGER  TO  EXECUTE  A  GENERAL SERVICE AGREEMENT WITH XANTRION, INC., FOR INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SERVICES  FROM  NOVEMBER  1,  2025,  THROUGH  OCTOBER  31,  2026,  IN  AN AMOUNT NOT TO EXCEED $1,207,200.

## RECOMMENDATION:

Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute a general service agreement with Xantrion, Inc., for information technology services from November 1, 2025, through October 31, 2026, in an amount not to exceed $1,207,200.

## BACKGROUND:

In May 2019, the Department of Digital Service and Open Government published a Request for Proposals for a managed-service provider to address the City's information technology systems and assembled an evaluation  team  with  representatives  from  the  Police,  Fire,  Library  &amp;  Recreation,  and  Public  Works departments. The City received eight proposals. At the end of the evaluation process, Xantrion was selected as the preferred vendor to partner with the City by providing the following services:

- Technical support ('help desk')
- Network, server, and database administration
- Equipment purchasing
- User account management
- Data backup and recovery
- Network monitoring and security

The City entered into an agreement with Xantrion in October 2019 for managed information technology (IT)  services  across  all  City  departments.  The  City  Council has  approved  renewing  that  one-year agreement for the past five years.
